title: Optimize walkthrough: Quant profiles INT8/FP8 - Elysium AI
summary: Redwood SE walked through INT8 vs FP8 quantization tradeoffs using Optimize. Focus on quality vs latency curves, example benchmarks on 8k context. Customer wants a POC to validate FP8 on their LLM and guidance on fallback to INT8 for throughput-sensitive endpoints.
next_steps: Alex to send tailored pricing and quant benchmark spreadsheet
Priya to share Optimize profile export and recommended configs
Customer to provide 2 representative prompts and sample model weights metadata
action_items: Alex Kim | Send pricing + quant benchmark spreadsheet | 2026-10-09
Priya Desai | Export and share Optimize quant profiles + sample run logs | 2026-10-08

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-05T15:00Z (62m) - Optimize walkthrough for quantization profiles
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marco Ortega (Redwood), Sara Nguyen (CTO, Elysium AI), Tom Keller (ML Eng), Ravi Patel (Infra), Maya Lopez (Product)

00:00 Alex: Alright everyone, thanks for joining, we know folks are busy. Quick agenda - walkthrough of INT8 vs FP8 profiles in Redwood Optimize, show quality vs latency curves, cover batching/KV cache impacts and then POC scope. Is that good?
00:06 Sara: Yeah that works. We mostly want to know if FP8 actually buys us accuracy and where it breaks on our safety evals.
00:12 Priya: Totally, we'll show both synthetic and customer-like prompts. Quick note - some of the names in the reports are auto-transcribed so you'll see things like K V cash instead of KV cache.
00:20 Tom: That's fine. Also, our production goal is p95 < 200ms for short chat and 50 tokens per second for longer generation, curious where FP8 sits.
00:28 Alex: Great. Priya, can you take us through the Optimize profile?
00:31 Priya: Yep, jumping in. (background typing) So first slide, profile summary - we ran three quant profiles: FP16 baseline, INT8, and FP8 mixed-mode. For this model - 7B encoder-decoder variant - we saw INT8 gives ~1.6x throughput vs FP16 with modest quality delta, FP8 lands in between, often giving close-to-FP16 quality with ~1.3-1.8x latency improvements depending on layer-fusion and kernel choice.
00:55 Sara: Can you explain "mixed-mode" for FP8? Is that where critical layers stay in FP16?
00:59 Priya: Exactly. Mixed-mode keeps attention & norm ops in higher precision and quantizes matmuls where safe. In some runs we keep first and last layer unquantized which recovers a chunk of quality.
01:10 Tom: Our concern is hallucinations and instruction-following degradation with aggressive quantization. Did you run evals on instruction fidelity?
01:16 Priya: Yes, we ran an instruction-following eval set and a safety/regression set. INT8 had a measurable drop - certain prompts with long context showed 3-5% drop in exact-match metrics. FP8 mixed-mode reduced that delta to ~1% or less, so that's why FP8 is attractive if you need quality guardrails.
01:33 Ravi: What about memory and batch size impact? We're constrained on GPU memory in on-prem racks.
01:38 Priya: FP8 reduces memory footprint vs FP16 and sometimes even INT8 depending on kernel packing. You get more room for larger batch sizes or longer KV cache. That said, INT8 kernels can be more throughput-optimized on some hardware and give better singleshot latency for small batch sizes.
01:53 Marco: Quick product note - Optimize will recommend profiles based on your workload traces; you can also pin a profile per route and define fallback to INT8 when latency SLO is at risk.
02:03 Maya: Nice. How deterministic are these numbers? Our latency distribution matters.
02:07 Priya: We provide p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec curves. The demos use a mix of sample traffic - e.g., conversational short-turns and long-form completions. There's variance across sequence length. For short requests (<64 tokens) INT8 often gives the best p95; for longer sequences FP8's memory savings help throughput and reduce tails.
02:27 Tom: Could you show the quality vs latency plot you mentioned earlier?
02:30 Priya: Sure - (screen share) here's a curve: x-axis latency (ms), y-axis QA accuracy. FP16 baseline at left-high quality, INT8 shifts right-lower quality but lower latency, FP8 sits close to FP16 in quality but slightly right for latency savings. Important caveat: models with sensitive layer norms can be more brittle with INT8.
02:50 Sara: Do you have real example generations to compare? Synthetic metrics are good but we need qualitative look.
02:54 Priya: We do. I'll read a short prompt pair - note auto-transcription might mangle punctuation. Prompt A: "Summarize the user request and list follow up questions." FP16 output: [clean concise summary]. INT8 output: [summary with a couple ambiguous phrases]. FP8 output: very close to FP16, slight terseness.
03:12 Tom: That matches our internal small-scale experiments. We saw INT8 more likely to truncate or omit edge-case safety mentions.
03:18 Priya: Yep. For safety-critical outputs we recommend either FP8 mixed-mode or INT8 with eval gating - e.g., run a cheap safety classifier on the output.
03:27 Ravi: On the infra side, what are requirements to run FP8 kernels on our on-prem fleet? We run A100 Gen1 and some H100s.
03:33 Priya: H100s have first-class FP8 kernel support with our runtime; A100 Gen1 support depends on compiler/kernels and you may see less benefit. For H100 we observed up to 1.8x token/sec gains with FP8. On A100s INT8 optimized kernels often win. We'll include hardware-specific benchmark tables in the spreadsheet.
03:51 Sara: Encryption and KMS - any changes to keys or certs when we run dedicated/private?
03:55 Alex: No changes needed to your keys; Redwood Private integrates with your KMS/HSM. We keep audit logs and key usage separate for dedicated tenants. We'll share our SOC2 and architecture docs.
04:05 Maya: What's the fallback story? If we push FP8 and see regressions in production how do we roll back?
04:09 Marco: You can pin routes to a profile and Redwood Console supports canary rollouts and automatic fallback to a compatible profile (e.g., INT8 or FP16) when latency or quality regressions cross thresholds. That works across hosted and private deployments.
04:22 Tom: For POC - we want to run FP8 mixed-mode on two workloads: a short-chat endpoint and a long-form summarization endpoint. Can Redwood run the tests or do we run them locally?
04:31 Alex: Either. For Private POC we can run the job with your weights in your environment (we provide a runner) or we can run against a sanitized copy in our dedicated infra. Both have pros/cons - on-prem gives exact network/hardware fidelity, dedicated lets us instrument more easily.
04:46 Ravi: On security I'd prefer on-prem run, but we may let Redwood run initial benchmarks on dedicated infra to iterate faster.
04:52 Priya: Sounds good. We'll prepare two Optimize profiles and a comparison spreadsheet showing p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and QA delta vs baseline plus sample generations.
04:59 Sara: Timeline: we want initial results within a week. Is that realistic?
05:03 Alex: Yes, if we get your prompts and model meta by Friday we can schedule the runs next week and follow up with results by 10/12.
05:11 Tom: One more technical - what about KV cache behavior with quantization? We rely on long context and prefix caching.
05:17 Priya: Great question. Quantization doesn't change KV semantics but memory footprint changes mean you can keep larger prefix caches in-memory. Note some kernels compress packed kv differently; Optimize shows effective cache size metrics. For very long contexts we sometimes prefer FP8 because it frees up memory for kv persistence which helps latency on repeated prompts.
05:38 Ravi: Any known gotchas with sharded attention or tensor parallelism?
05:41 Priya: Sharding doesn't break quantization but can expose kernel incompatibilities across TP implementations. We test common TP setups; for custom sharding we recommend running our small validation harness.
05:51 Maya: Pricing - does FP8 affect cost?
05:54 Alex: It can. FP8 that lets you fit larger batches or reduce GPU count will lower unit cost. We'll model cost-per-1k-tokens in the spreadsheet for each profile and hardware type.
06:05 Sara: Ok let's recap and next steps.
06:09 Alex: Recap - Redwood will: send pricing and benchmark spreadsheet (Alex); Priya to export Optimize profiles and run initial comparison logs; schedule POC kickoff for 10/12 or 10/13; Elysium to send two prompt sets and model metadata and confirm hardware set.
06:25 Sara: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

Action notes appended: Alex: send pricing + spreadsheet. Priya: export profiles and logs. Ravi: share perf targets.

References mentioned: Optimize profile export, quant-bench.xlsx (will be shared), SOC2 and security architecture doc (link to be shared), sample generations (in spreadsheet).

End of transcript.
